summary: Matthew is an internally anonymous Greek Gospel that narrates Jesus as Messiah, son of David and Abraham, Emmanuel, authoritative teacher, healer, crucified king, and risen Lord. It joins Israel's Scriptures, kingdom proclamation, five large discourses, contested discipleship, passion, resurrection, and a mission to all nations while requiring careful historical, Jewish-contextual, textual, and ethical interpretation.
historical_context: Matthew reflects the Roman eastern Mediterranean and a deeply Jewish scriptural world. The narrative ranges through Galilee, Judea, and Jerusalem under Herodian and Roman rule; its final literary setting is often placed after 70 CE, but exact date, city, author, audience, and institutional relationship to other Jewish groups remain debated. Rural agriculture, fishing, tolls, debt, patronage, household authority, purity practices, synagogues, the Jerusalem temple, imperial taxation, crucifixion, and burial belong to the worlds the Gospel evokes.
ancient_near_east_context: This context is not directly applicable as Matthew's historical period. Its genealogy, exodus patterning, royal and prophetic language, covenant vocabulary, wisdom, lament, and scriptural citations nevertheless receive older Israelite traditions through Hebrew and Greek textual forms.
hebraic_worldview: Matthew reads Jesus within Israel's story: Abraham, David, exile, Moses, Torah, prophets, wisdom, temple, covenant, mercy, justice, resurrection, and restoration. The Gospel's fulfillment language is a Jewish scriptural practice and must not be turned into a claim that Judaism, Jews, Torah, or Israel are obsolete.
second_temple_context: The Gospel assumes Jewish debates about Torah, purity, Sabbath, prayer, almsgiving, fasting, divorce, vows, tithes, resurrection, messiahship, temple, and communal discipline. Pharisees, Sadducees, scribes, priests, crowds, disciples, and Jesus are not interchangeable representatives of all Jews; narrated conflicts must be located within diverse first-century Jewish life and Matthew's later rhetorical setting.
canonical_context: Matthew opens the New Testament canon in common Christian ordering, repeatedly cites Israel's Scriptures, shares extensive material with Mark and Luke, and is received alongside John, Acts, Paul, Hebrews, James, and Revelation. Canonical comparison can illuminate shared traditions and differences, but it must not erase each text's voice or convert later synthesis into Matthew's historical meaning.
later_christian_reception: Matthew became exceptionally influential in catechesis, liturgy, ethics, Christology, Trinitarian theology, ecclesiology, art, mission, monasticism, politics, and social reform. The same Gospel has also been weaponized for anti-Judaism, deicide accusations, coercive mission, colonialism, clerical abuse, misogyny, disability stigma, economic exploitation, and apocalyptic fear, making reception history ethically indispensable.
literary_context: Matthew is a sustained Gospel narrative with genealogy and infancy scenes, recurring fulfillment formulas, alternating deed and discourse collections, repeated summaries, geographic turns, controversy sequences, passion and resurrection. Five discourse-ending formulas at 7:28, 11:1, 13:53, 19:1, and 26:1 support a major compositional observation, but they do not by themselves prove one Mosaic blueprint or a single rigid outline.
covenantal_significance: Matthew presents Jesus' life and teaching as fulfillment of Israel's Scriptures and speaks of covenant blood at the final meal. Christian readings connect this to covenant renewal and the inclusion of nations, but such readings cannot cancel God's relation to Israel, erase Jewish covenantal life, or authorize domination.
authorship_positions: The extant narrative does not name its author; the title according to Matthew belongs to manuscript and reception history.
Early Christian tradition associated Matthew with the apostle and toll collector, but the relationship between canonical Matthew and Papias's report about logia in a Hebrew dialect is disputed.

Many critical scholars infer a Greek-writing Jewish follower of Jesus or a learned Jesus-group setting that used Mark and additional traditions; biography, profession, location, and group boundaries remain unrecoverable.
Minority positions defend direct apostolic authorship, different source relationships, or earlier dates; these are reception and scholarly positions rather than facts stated by the Gospel.
date_ranges: Often dated approximately 70-100 CE in modern scholarship
Many proposals cluster in the 80s or 90s CE, without a secure exact year
Earlier and later proposals exist; temple-destruction language, Markan dependence, and early reception are interpreted differently
original_audience: Unknown readers or hearers conversant with Greek, Israel's Scriptures, Jewish practices and disputes, and the Roman world; the text addresses both Israel-focused and all-nations horizons, but no single city, ethnicity, congregation, or clean synagogue-church separation can be demonstrated.
historical_setting: A Greek-speaking Jewish and Greco-Roman environment remembering Jesus' activity in early first-century Galilee and Judea while shaping a Gospel amid later first-century debates, commonly but not certainly after Jerusalem's temple destruction.
canonical_role: Matthew supplies a canonical Gospel witness to Jesus' genealogy, teaching, deeds, passion, resurrection, and commission. Its placement first among the Gospels has amplified its role as a bridge from Israel's Scriptures to the New Testament, though canonical order is not proof of composition date.

new_testament_connections: Mark supplies the closest sustained narrative parallel under the widely held Markan-priority model.
Luke shares substantial sayings and narrative material while arranging and wording it differently.
John offers distinct yet intersecting witnesses to Jesus, passion, resurrection, mission, and Father-Son language.
Acts and the letters provide early Christian mission, baptism, community, Torah, cross, and resurrection comparanda without functioning as Matthew's automatic commentary.

interpretive_notes.note: The Gospel is internally anonymous; the later title and Papias tradition are important evidence, but their relationship to the extant Greek narrative does not settle the author's biography.
interpretive_notes.rationale: Narrative anonymity is observable while attribution arguments depend on contested external evidence.

interpretive_notes.note: Papias's report concerns Matthew arranging logia in a Hebrew dialect, but the meanings of logia, dialect, and interpretation and the identity of the work remain disputed.
interpretive_notes.rationale: The fragment survives indirectly and does not map unambiguously onto canonical Matthew.

interpretive_notes.note: A date around 70-100 CE is common but not textually explicit; temple-destruction language, Markan dependence, and reception establish arguments rather than an exact year.
interpretive_notes.rationale: Multiple indirect indicators support a range, not precision.

interpretive_notes.note: Antioch, Syria more broadly, Galilee, and other eastern Mediterranean settings have been proposed, but the Gospel names no place of composition.
interpretive_notes.rationale: Cultural fit and reception cannot identify a city securely.

interpretive_notes.note: Literary dependence on Mark is widely judged probable because of extensive sequence and wording agreements, while Q, direct use of Luke, oral performance, and other source models remain debated.
interpretive_notes.rationale: The data demand a relationship but do not yield one uncontested reconstruction.

interpretive_notes.note: Matthew's genealogy is a crafted theological genealogy in three stated groups of fourteen; omissions and counting questions warn against treating it as a complete modern registry.
interpretive_notes.rationale: Matthew states the pattern and comparison with biblical genealogies reveals selectivity.

interpretive_notes.note: Interpretations of Tamar, Rahab, Ruth, Bathsheba identified through Uriah, and Mary include irregular unions, Gentile associations, divine providence, danger, agency, and anticipation; no single label explains every woman.
interpretive_notes.rationale: The women and their scriptural stories resist one reduction.

interpretive_notes.note: Matthew narrates Mary's conception from the Holy Spirit and cites Greek Isaiah 7:14; historical, biological, confessional, and textual claims must be distinguished.
interpretive_notes.rationale: What the narrator claims is clear, while historical and doctrinal judgments use different warrants.

interpretive_notes.note: The magi are eastern specialists, not numbered or called kings by Matthew; later names, number three, royal status, and racial iconography belong to reception history.
interpretive_notes.rationale: The text supplies gifts and a group but not later biographical details.

interpretive_notes.note: Astronomical, astrological, miraculous, literary, and scriptural readings of the star compete; Matthew does not provide enough data for a confident modern identification.
interpretive_notes.rationale: The narrated star behaves within a theological story rather than a scientific report.

interpretive_notes.note: Herod's brutality is historically plausible in broad outline, but Matthew's massacre of Bethlehem's children lacks independent attestation and its scale cannot be reconstructed.
interpretive_notes.rationale: Independent evidence illuminates Herod without verifying this event.

interpretive_notes.note: The Egypt, son, Rachel, and Nazorean formulas combine scriptural voices and narrative geography; 'he shall be called a Nazorean' has no single verbatim Hebrew Bible source.
interpretive_notes.rationale: The formulas are explicit but their compositional logic differs.

interpretive_notes.note: Jesus' baptism joins solidarity, righteousness, Spirit, heavenly voice, and sonship; later Trinitarian or sacramental readings are reception, not exhaustive historical description.
interpretive_notes.rationale: Narrative features support theology while later doctrinal synthesis must be labeled.

interpretive_notes.note: The temptation scenes quote Deuteronomy and portray faithful sonship; they are narrated theological conflict and cannot establish a clinical description of evil or mental illness.
interpretive_notes.rationale: Scriptural dialogue controls the scene's literary presentation.

interpretive_notes.note: Kingdom of heaven is Matthew's characteristic expression for God's reign and does not simply mean a disembodied place after death.
interpretive_notes.rationale: Narrative uses include present action, future hope, ethics, judgment, and divine rule.

interpretive_notes.note: The five discourse endings are observable, but claims that Matthew deliberately reproduces five books of Moses range from plausible to speculative.
interpretive_notes.rationale: Formal repetition is firmer than a specific symbolic blueprint.

interpretive_notes.note: Matthew 5:17-20 affirms Torah and Prophets while the antitheses interpret commands with distinctive authority; abolition, simple repetition, and replacement readings all underdescribe the tension.
interpretive_notes.rationale: Fulfillment and intensified interpretation must be held together.

interpretive_notes.note: The repeated 'you heard ... but I say' form is not evidence that Judaism taught murder, lust, divorce, falsehood, revenge, or hatred as virtues.
interpretive_notes.rationale: Jesus disputes interpretations within Jewish ethical worlds, not a caricature of Jewish morality.

interpretive_notes.note: Enemy love and non-retaliation have inspired transformative nonviolence, but they cannot require victims to remain exposed to assault, conceal abuse, or surrender lawful protection.
interpretive_notes.rationale: Ethical application must protect vulnerable people and distinguish personal vengeance from safety.

interpretive_notes.note: The Lord's Prayer in Matthew has ancient textual and liturgical variation, especially the doxology; translation and worship tradition should not be confused with one recoverable wording in every witness.
interpretive_notes.rationale: Manuscript and liturgical transmission produced known differences.

interpretive_notes.note: Almsgiving, prayer, and fasting are Jewish practices Matthew's Jesus assumes; the critique targets performative status seeking, not Judaism or embodied ritual as such.
interpretive_notes.rationale: The instructions begin with expectation that disciples practice them.

interpretive_notes.note: Gehenna language draws on the Valley of Hinnom and judgment traditions; later maps of hell exceed what each Matthean saying specifies and must not be used for terror or coercion.
interpretive_notes.rationale: Metaphorical and eschatological language has a reception history beyond its local sayings.

interpretive_notes.note: Matthew's healing and exorcism stories express compassion, authority, restoration, and contested ancient causation; they do not equate disability or mental illness with sin, demons, weak faith, or moral failure.
interpretive_notes.rationale: Ancient narrative categories cannot be imposed as modern diagnoses.

interpretive_notes.note: Archaeology contextualizes rural Galilee, Jerusalem, purity installations, economy, and burial, but it neither proves nor disproves individual miracles.
interpretive_notes.rationale: Material evidence and narrated supernatural claims answer different questions.

interpretive_notes.note: The mission discourse initially focuses on Israel; the final commission names all nations. Interpreters debate narrative sequence, Israel's continuing place, and Gentile inclusion without warrant for replacement theology.
interpretive_notes.rationale: Both horizons are stated and neither authorizes erasing Israel.

interpretive_notes.note: Parables reveal and conceal within Matthew's Isaiah-shaped narrative; they are not timeless codes with one-to-one meanings for every detail or proof that outsiders are permanently rejected.
interpretive_notes.rationale: Narrative setting, audience, explanation, and reception vary.

interpretive_notes.note: The Canaanite woman scene stages ethnic boundary, silence, insult, persistence, discipleship failure, and healing; attempts to excuse the dog's saying must not erase the woman's danger, agency, or the text's disturbance.
interpretive_notes.rationale: The narrative's resolution does not make its unequal exchange harmless.

interpretive_notes.note: Peter's confession, rock, keys, binding, and loosing remain disputed across historical, lexical, Catholic, Orthodox, Protestant, and ecclesial readings.
interpretive_notes.rationale: The wordplay is clear while referent and institutional consequences are contested.

interpretive_notes.note: Binding and loosing can evoke authoritative interpretation and communal decisions, but Matthew does not provide a blank check for leaders to control conscience, property, sexuality, safety, or access to God.
interpretive_notes.rationale: Authority is narratively bounded by service, care for little ones, and accountability.

interpretive_notes.note: Matthew 18's church discipline sequence aims at truth, restoration, and communal responsibility; it cannot license secrecy, retaliation, surveillance, shunning dependents, obstruction of justice, or clerical abuse.
interpretive_notes.rationale: Safe application must respect legal duties and protect those at risk.

interpretive_notes.note: Unlimited forgiveness rejects vengeance and scorekeeping, but it does not require trust, access, reconciliation, silence, or removal of consequences when an offender is unsafe or unrepentant.
interpretive_notes.rationale: Forgiveness and restored relationship are distinguishable ethical categories.

interpretive_notes.note: Matthew's divorce sayings and exception clauses are textually and ethically disputed; they must not coerce continued exposure to violence, shame divorced people, or place unilateral burdens on women.
interpretive_notes.rationale: Ancient household law and modern safety require careful distinction.

interpretive_notes.note: The eunuch saying may refer to birth, human action, and voluntary celibacy in ancient categories; it cannot justify genital harm, compulsory celibacy, anti-intersex stigma, or anti-LGBTQ coercion.
interpretive_notes.rationale: The saying is compressed and its application has harmed embodied minorities.

interpretive_notes.note: The rich young man, laborers, debts, talents, and judgment scenes expose wealth, need, stewardship, and unequal power in different genres; they do not teach prosperity guarantees or romanticize poverty.
interpretive_notes.rationale: Economic images must be interpreted within agrarian inequality and each scene's rhetoric.

interpretive_notes.note: Slave and master imagery reflects ancient coercive institutions; theological analogy must not normalize enslavement, torture, trafficking, workplace exploitation, or authoritarian leadership.
interpretive_notes.rationale: Metaphor does not morally endorse the social violence it presupposes.

interpretive_notes.note: The ransom saying interprets Jesus' service and death; substitution, liberation, victory, martyrdom, and covenant readings require canonical and doctrinal argument beyond the single term lytron.
interpretive_notes.rationale: The saying is explicit but later atonement systems are broader syntheses.

interpretive_notes.note: The entry and temple action invoke royal, prophetic, and judgment traditions. Calling the event a cleansing can prejudge its target and must not portray Jewish worship as inherently corrupt.
interpretive_notes.rationale: Sign action, commerce, access, and temple judgment receive multiple readings.

interpretive_notes.note: Render-to-Caesar and temple-tax scenes occur within overlapping imperial and sacred economies; they are not simple endorsements of every government, tax, revolt, or church-state arrangement.
interpretive_notes.rationale: Different taxes and narrative traps require contextual distinction.

interpretive_notes.note: Matthew's woes attack named leaders in intra-Jewish polemic and also expose hypocrisy among disciples and later churches; Pharisees are not a synonym for Jews, Judaism, legalism, or all religious leaders.
interpretive_notes.rationale: Historical diversity and reception history prohibit collective stereotyping.

interpretive_notes.note: The cumulative blood-guilt rhetoric in Matthew 23 must not be transferred to Jewish descendants or modern communities; inherited collective blame contradicts responsible historical reading.
interpretive_notes.rationale: Rhetorical accusation is not a biological or perpetual legal sentence.

interpretive_notes.note: Jerusalem's lament holds judgment and protective desire together; it cannot authorize hatred of Jerusalem's residents, Palestinians, Israelis, Jews, Muslims, Christians, Arabs, or any modern claimant.
interpretive_notes.rationale: Ancient personified-city rhetoric is not a modern territorial deed.

interpretive_notes.note: Matthew 24 intertwines temple destruction, tribulation, Son of Man imagery, watchfulness, and coming. Proposals about sequence, fulfillment, and parousia remain disputed.
interpretive_notes.rationale: The discourse moves among horizons without a universally accepted timetable.

interpretive_notes.note: 'This generation' has several proposed referents, and the abomination draws on Daniel and crisis memory; neither phrase securely names a modern nation, technology, vaccine, leader, or date.
interpretive_notes.rationale: Lexical and historical uncertainty rules out confident newspaper decoding.

interpretive_notes.note: No one knows the day or hour functions against date-setting; apocalyptic teaching cannot justify panic, conspiracy theories, stockpiling at others' expense, or neglect of ordinary responsibility.
interpretive_notes.rationale: Watchfulness in the discourse is ethical fidelity, not timetable mastery.

interpretive_notes.note: The ten virgins, talents, and sheep-and-goats scenes use different images of readiness, entrusted responsibility, and judgment; characters and assets are not automatic allegorical ciphers.
interpretive_notes.rationale: Genre and narrative sequence constrain but do not eliminate interpretation.

interpretive_notes.note: Matthew 25:31-46 has been read as judgment of nations, treatment of missionaries, care for vulnerable people, or Christ's solidarity with the least; the identity of 'these' and 'brothers' remains disputed.
interpretive_notes.rationale: The ethical demand is forceful while referents are debated.

interpretive_notes.note: The anointing woman's act is interpreted by Jesus as preparation for burial and promised worldwide remembrance; readings must preserve her agency rather than use her only as a symbol for male actors.
interpretive_notes.rationale: The narrator gives her action interpretive prominence despite leaving her unnamed.

interpretive_notes.note: The meal's 'blood of the covenant' evokes scriptural covenant and interprets Jesus' death; Eucharistic presence, sacrifice, and sacramental efficacy are later denominational debates.
interpretive_notes.rationale: Narrated words ground reception but do not settle all later sacramental doctrine.

interpretive_notes.note: Judas is a narrated betrayer whose motives and final responsibility are not reducible to ethnicity, divine predestination, mental illness, or a stereotype of Jews.
interpretive_notes.rationale: Matthew narrates actions and remorse but not a complete psychology.

interpretive_notes.note: Gethsemane holds Jesus' distress, prayer, obedience, companionship, and abandonment; it should not be used to shame trauma responses, fear, grief, or requests for help.
interpretive_notes.rationale: The scene dignifies anguish rather than depicting emotion as faithlessness.

interpretive_notes.note: Matthew distributes agency in Jesus' death among Judas, priestly and council leaders, crowds, Pilate, Roman soldiers, and imperial execution; it does not permit shifting Roman crucifixion onto all Jews.
interpretive_notes.rationale: Narrative roles and historical Roman power must both remain visible.

interpretive_notes.note: 'His blood be on us and on our children' is crowd speech within Matthew's trial narrative and cannot authorize deicide, collective Jewish guilt, hereditary curse, persecution, or violence.
interpretive_notes.rationale: Its lethal anti-Jewish reception makes explicit rejection of collective application mandatory.

interpretive_notes.note: Pilate's handwashing does not erase Roman legal and military responsibility, and Pilate's wife does not convert the Roman household into an innocent counterweight to guilty Jews.
interpretive_notes.rationale: Narrative symbolism must be read against imperial execution power.

interpretive_notes.note: Darkness, torn curtain, earthquake, opened tombs, raised saints, and the centurion's confession are narrated signs; historicity, symbolism, apocalyptic texture, and intertexts must be distinguished.
interpretive_notes.rationale: Textual presence is certain while genre and external verification are debated.

interpretive_notes.note: Roman crucifixion was public state violence. Christian proclamation of the cross cannot glorify torture, demand passive submission to abuse, or aestheticize victims' trauma.
interpretive_notes.rationale: Historical context and trauma-aware ethics resist sacralizing coercion.

interpretive_notes.note: Mary Magdalene and the other Mary witness death, burial, empty tomb, angelic announcement, and the risen Jesus; their narrative authority must not be erased by later restrictions on women.
interpretive_notes.rationale: Matthew repeatedly positions them as observers and commissioned speakers.

interpretive_notes.note: The guard story is distinctive to Matthew and participates in dispute over the empty tomb; its historical setting, apologetic function, and relation to later polemic remain contested.
interpretive_notes.rationale: The narrative exists, but no independent source verifies its arrangement.

interpretive_notes.note: Resurrection is Matthew's narrated and theological claim; historical arguments, confessional affirmation, visionary models, and naturalistic rejection operate with different assumptions.
interpretive_notes.rationale: The record must state the text's claim without pretending later debate is resolved.

interpretive_notes.note: Worship and doubt or hesitation coexist among the disciples on the Galilean mountain; doubt is not erased from discipleship and should not be punished or silenced.
interpretive_notes.rationale: Distazo can express hesitation, and the commission addresses this mixed group.

interpretive_notes.note: The Great Commission joins Jesus' authority, disciple-making, baptism, teaching, all nations, and enduring presence; it cannot authorize coercive conversion, colonial mission, forced baptism, cultural erasure, conquest, or religious violence.
interpretive_notes.rationale: Commissioned teaching under Jesus' presence is incompatible with violating persons and peoples.

interpretive_notes.note: The Father-Son-Holy Spirit wording of Matthew 28:19 is supported by the extant Greek manuscript tradition used in critical texts; Eusebian citation patterns and early reception are discussed, but claims of a late Nicene manuscript insertion lack surviving Greek manuscript support.
interpretive_notes.rationale: Text-critical evidence and later doctrinal interpretation must not be conflated.

interpretive_notes.note: Matthew 28:19 is triadic language important to later Trinitarian theology, but the fully articulated conciliar doctrine is a later systematic synthesis rather than a term Matthew states.
interpretive_notes.rationale: Historical reception distinguishes textual formula from later doctrinal grammar.

interpretive_notes.note: Ancient versions, patristic citations, papyri, Sinaiticus, and Vaticanus witness a transmitted textual history with variants; no surviving manuscript is Matthew's autograph.
interpretive_notes.rationale: Material witnesses are copies from different periods and textual histories.

interpretive_notes.note: Matthew's fulfillment formulas use Hebrew Bible, Septuagint, mixed forms, and interpretive wording; 'fulfilled' does not always mean a one-to-one prediction consciously awaiting Jesus.
interpretive_notes.rationale: Citation techniques include typology, rereading, analogy, and narrative correspondence.

interpretive_notes.note: Matthew remains a Jewish text in language, Scripture, practice, and debate even where its polemic marks contested group identity; a simple Judaism-versus-Christianity split is historically anachronistic.
interpretive_notes.rationale: Late first-century identities and partings were diverse, local, and unfinished.

interpretive_notes.note: Calling Matthew's audience a single 'community' can be a useful model but should not turn inferred readers into a fully reconstructed institution, leadership crisis, synagogue expulsion, or city.
interpretive_notes.rationale: Texts imply audiences but do not supply an ethnography.

interpretive_notes.note: Roman Palestine's agrarian inequality, taxation, tenancy, household hierarchy, and temple economy illuminate Matthew's debt, labor, wealth, toll, and patronage images without reducing them to modern capitalism or socialism.
interpretive_notes.rationale: Responsible analogy identifies both continuities and historical differences.

interpretive_notes.note: Matthew's children and 'little ones' are not merely metaphors; applications must prioritize children's safety and never spiritualize grooming, corporal violence, neglect, forced estrangement, or concealment of abuse.
interpretive_notes.rationale: Protective interpretation follows the Gospel's warnings against causing harm.

interpretive_notes.note: Purity controversy cannot be used to stigmatize Jewish practice, menstruation, disease, disability, foodways, or bodies; Matthew's argument concerns authority and moral defilement within a Jewish debate.
interpretive_notes.rationale: Historical context and disability-aware ethics resist bodily contempt.

interpretive_notes.note: Matthew's ecological images of seeds, soils, birds, lilies, storms, animals, vineyards, and harvest are literary and material; dominion or judgment readings cannot excuse ecological destruction or animal cruelty.
interpretive_notes.rationale: Agrarian imagery depends on living land and creatures rather than licensing their exploitation.

interpretive_notes.note: Modern application must distinguish ancient Judea and Galilee from modern political identities; Matthew grants no territorial title, ethnic curse, racial hierarchy, or partisan platform.
interpretive_notes.rationale: Direct geopolitical mapping collapses two millennia of history and fuels harm.

interpretive_notes.note: Black, womanist, feminist, postcolonial, disability-aware, trauma-aware, and economically situated readings can expose harms and silenced voices; they are accountable interpretive perspectives, not substitutes for textual and historical evidence.
interpretive_notes.rationale: Situated reception expands questions while remaining open to evidence and critique.

claims.claim: The extant Gospel is a Greek narrative whose internal narrator does not identify an author.
claims.rationale: The continuous Greek text lacks an internal authorial self-identification.

claims.claim: Association with Matthew the apostle is early Christian reception, while its precise relation to Papias and the extant Gospel remains disputed.
claims.rationale: External testimony exists but is indirect and textually ambiguous.

claims.claim: Many scholars date Matthew approximately 70-100 CE, often after Jerusalem's temple destruction, but no exact year is textually stated.
claims.rationale: Dating depends on literary dependence, historical allusion, and reception rather than a colophon.

claims.claim: Matthew shares extensive sequence and wording with Mark and Luke; Markan priority is widely held but source and publication models remain contested.
claims.rationale: Verbal and sequential agreements require explanation, while no single model commands unanimity.

claims.claim: Matthew 1:1-17 structures Jesus' ancestry from Abraham through David and exile in three announced groups of fourteen.
claims.rationale: The names and numerical statement are explicit, though counting and omissions require interpretation.

claims.claim: Tamar, Rahab, Ruth, Uriah's wife, and Mary receive unusual genealogical attention whose collective significance is debated.
claims.rationale: Their presence is explicit but explanatory theories vary.

claims.claim: Matthew narrates conception from the Holy Spirit and interprets it through Greek Isaiah 7:14's parthenos and Emmanuel.
claims.rationale: Narrative and citation are explicit; historical and doctrinal evaluation differs.

claims.claim: Matthew narrates eastern magi, a star, gifts, Herod's alarm, and worship of the child without numbering the magi or calling them kings.
claims.rationale: Narrated details are clear while external verification and later expansions differ.

claims.claim: Matthew alone narrates Herod's killing of Bethlehem's young children; broad Herodian brutality is independently contextualized, but this event is not independently attested.
claims.rationale: Narrative attestation and independent historical evidence must be distinguished.

claims.claim: Matthew repeatedly frames events with citations and fulfillment formulas drawing on varied Hebrew and Greek scriptural forms.
claims.rationale: Citation practice is extensive, while textual sources and hermeneutical models vary by passage.

claims.claim: Matthew presents baptism and wilderness testing as Spirit-marked sonship interpreted through scriptural voices and Deuteronomy.
claims.rationale: Narrative sequence, voice, Spirit, and quotations are explicit.

claims.claim: Jesus' public proclamation begins with repentance because the kingdom of heaven has drawn near.
claims.rationale: The wording is explicit; temporal and theological scope are debated.

claims.claim: Five repeated discourse-ending formulas organize large teaching collections without proving one universally accepted symbolic outline.
claims.rationale: Formula repetition is observable; Mosaic or Pentateuchal symbolism is inferred.

claims.claim: Matthew 5:17-20 rejects abolishing Torah and Prophets while authorizing a demanding interpretation of righteousness.
claims.rationale: The affirmation is explicit while fulfillment and continuing legal scope are debated.

claims.claim: The antitheses address murder, adultery, divorce, oaths, retaliation, and enemies through Jesus' authoritative interpretation rather than a wholesale contrast between Christianity and Judaism.
claims.rationale: The topics and formula recur within an explicitly Torah-affirming discourse.

claims.claim: Matthew 6 places almsgiving, prayer, fasting, possessions, and trust within a critique of public status performance.
claims.rationale: The practices and critique are explicit; the Lord's Prayer doxology varies in transmission.

claims.claim: Matthew's summaries and stories present Jesus teaching, proclaiming, healing, and exorcising amid ancient understandings of bodies and spirits.
claims.rationale: Narrative claims are explicit; historical causation and modern diagnosis cannot be inferred directly.

claims.claim: Matthew juxtaposes an initial mission focused on Israel with a concluding commission directed to all nations.
claims.rationale: Both horizons are explicit; their theological relation remains debated.

claims.claim: Matthew 13 gathers kingdom parables with audience changes, Isaiah hardening language, and selective explanations.
claims.rationale: The collection's form is clear while purpose, sources, and allegorical reach vary.

claims.claim: Matthew 15:21-28 narrates a Canaanite woman's persistent petition, a harsh boundary metaphor, Jesus' praise of her faith, and her daughter's healing.
claims.rationale: Narrative actions are explicit; ethical and theological construal is contested.

claims.claim: Matthew uniquely joins Peter's confession with rock, ekklesia, keys, and binding-loosing sayings that generated major ecclesial disputes.
claims.rationale: The sayings are explicit; referents and institutional consequences differ across traditions.

claims.claim: Matthew 18 links status reversal, protection of little ones, restoration, communal discipline, prayer, and forgiveness.
claims.rationale: The sequence is explicit, while institutional implementation and safeguards require judgment.

claims.claim: Matthew 19 preserves disputed divorce exception language and a threefold eunuch saying within teaching on marriage, children, and discipleship.
claims.rationale: The wording is explicit but legal, lexical, and applied meanings are contested.

claims.claim: Matthew's fields, fisheries, wages, debts, taxes, estates, slaves, patrons, and laborers resonate with an unequal agrarian Roman-Palestinian economy.
claims.rationale: Literary images align with independently reconstructed social institutions, though local details vary.

claims.claim: Matthew 20:28 connects Son of Man service, giving life, and ransom for many.
claims.rationale: The saying is explicit while later atonement theories extend beyond it.

claims.claim: Matthew narrates Jesus' royal entry, action in the temple, healings, children, and authority controversies through scriptural citations.
claims.rationale: Narrative sequence is explicit; event reconstruction and action's target are disputed.

claims.claim: Matthew distinguishes a temple-tax scene from the later tribute-to-Caesar controversy within layered fiscal and political contexts.
claims.rationale: The two scenes and payment forms differ; their precise post-70 resonances are debated.

claims.claim: Matthew 23 intensifies polemic against scribes and Pharisees while ending with lament over Jerusalem.
claims.rationale: The rhetoric is explicit, while historical targets and reception are contested.

claims.claim: Matthew 24-25 combines temple destruction, tribulation, Son of Man coming, uncertainty of timing, readiness, stewardship, and judgment.
claims.rationale: Themes are explicit but temporal relations and referents are disputed.

claims.claim: At the final meal Jesus identifies bread and cup with his body and covenant blood poured out for many for forgiveness.
claims.rationale: The sayings are explicit; sacramental and atonement doctrines differ.

claims.claim: Matthew portrays Jesus in deep distress praying for the cup to pass while submitting to the Father's will as disciples fail to watch.
claims.rationale: Narrative emotion, prayer, and disciple failure are explicit.

claims.claim: Matthew's passion assigns narrative agency to multiple Judean and Roman actors while crucifixion remains Roman state execution.
claims.rationale: The narrative names multiple actors and independent history establishes Roman execution power.

claims.claim: Matthew 27:25 records crowd speech about blood on 'us and our children'; its use for perpetual Jewish guilt or deicide is an abusive reception, not a valid historical inference.
claims.rationale: A bounded narrative utterance cannot ground hereditary guilt, and its violent reception is documented.

claims.claim: Matthew narrates darkness, curtain tearing, earthquake, opened tombs, raised saints, and a centurion's confession around Jesus' death.
claims.rationale: Textual narration is certain; historical and symbolic evaluation is disputed.

claims.claim: Mary Magdalene and the other Mary witness death, burial, empty tomb, angelic message, and the risen Jesus, who commissions them to tell the brothers.
claims.rationale: Their repeated witnessing and commissioned speech are explicit.

claims.claim: Matthew uniquely narrates a tomb guard, priestly negotiations, and a counterclaim that disciples stole the body.
claims.rationale: The story is explicit and distinctive, while historical reconstruction is uncertain.

claims.claim: Matthew concludes that Jesus was raised, met the women, and appeared to the eleven in Galilee.
claims.rationale: This is the Gospel's explicit claim; historical and confessional judgments differ.

claims.claim: On the Galilean mountain the disciples worship the risen Jesus while some or they also hesitate or doubt.
claims.rationale: Proskyneo and distazo are explicit; the subject and nuance of hesitation are discussed.

claims.claim: The risen Jesus claims all authority and commissions disciple-making among all nations through baptism, teaching, and promised presence.
claims.rationale: The commission is explicit; mission theology and practice are contested.

claims.claim: The extant Greek manuscript tradition supports baptism 'in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit,' later central to Trinitarian reception.
claims.rationale: Critical texts and surviving major witnesses contain the formula; later doctrine remains a reception development.

claims.claim: Matthew survives in early fragmentary papyri, fourth-century codices, later Greek manuscripts, ancient versions, and citations with recoverable textual variation.
claims.rationale: Cataloged material witnesses document transmission; none is an autograph.

claims.claim: Matthew's Scripture, Torah debate, practices, institutions, and actors locate it within diverse Jewish worlds even where later identity conflict shapes its polemic.
claims.rationale: Jewish texture is pervasive, while social location and boundary formation remain debated.

claims.claim: Herodian client rule, Roman provincial authority, taxation, elite power, and crucifixion frame Matthew's remembered first-century setting.
claims.rationale: Independent sources establish the political institutions, while narrative details need individual evaluation.

claims.claim: Matthew's polemic and passion have contributed to Christian anti-Judaism, supersessionism, and deicide accusations, requiring explicit safeguards in interpretation.
claims.rationale: Documented reception produced repeated stereotyping, exclusion, and violence.

claims.claim: Matthew's commission cannot ethically authorize coercive conversion, forced baptism, colonial domination, cultural erasure, or religious violence.
claims.rationale: Coercion contradicts responsible discipleship and ignores the commission's harmful reception.

claims.claim: Matthew cannot legitimately be used to excuse abuse, stigmatize disability or mental illness, enforce misogyny or anti-LGBTQ harm, blame poverty, set apocalyptic dates, or map ancient judgments onto modern peoples.
claims.rationale: Textual ethics, historical difference, and documented harms require explicit boundaries.

hermeneutical_lens.immediate_literary_context: Read each unit within Matthew's narrative sequence, speaker and audience, recurring vocabulary, discourse-deed pattern, geography, scriptural citations, and passion-resurrection conclusion.
hermeneutical_lens.book_context: Matthew integrates genealogy, infancy, kingdom proclamation, authoritative deeds, five major discourses, controversies, journey, passion, resurrection, and commission. No isolated saying should override that full movement.
hermeneutical_lens.canonical_context: Compare Israel's Scriptures, Mark, Luke, and other New Testament witnesses while identifying quotation, allusion, shared tradition, redaction, canonical resonance, and later synthesis separately.
hermeneutical_lens.covenant_context: Matthew's Abrahamic, Davidic, Mosaic, prophetic, and covenant-blood language is received christologically by Christians without canceling Israel, Torah, Jewish covenant, or Jewish peoplehood.
hermeneutical_lens.historical_context: Distinguish the narrated early first-century Herodian-Roman setting, the probable later first-century compositional horizon, and subsequent manuscript and reception history.
hermeneutical_lens.ancient_near_east_context: Not directly applicable as a period setting; use older Israelite and ancient Near Eastern context only where Matthew receives Hebrew Bible traditions.
hermeneutical_lens.second_temple_jewish_context: Locate Torah, purity, Sabbath, prayer, fasting, almsgiving, temple, synagogue, messiahship, resurrection, Pharisees, Sadducees, scribes, and priests within diverse Jewish debates.
hermeneutical_lens.original_audience: Treat Greek-literate hearers familiar with Jewish Scripture and Roman life as a bounded inference; do not invent one city, ethnicity, congregation, expulsion, or institutional split.
hermeneutical_lens.genre: Ancient biography and Gospel narrative containing genealogy, dream, citation, teaching, legal interpretation, healing, exorcism, parable, controversy, apocalypse, passion, empty tomb, appearance, and commission.
intertextual_connections: Test each fulfillment formula against its Hebrew Bible and Septuagint contexts.
Compare Matthew with Mark and Luke without harmonizing away differences.
Separate Danielic, Isaianic, Mosaic, Davidic, and prophetic echoes from modern prediction schemes.
Label later New Testament and doctrinal syntheses as canonical or reception moves.

discipleship, authority, service, forgiveness, and community
hermeneutical_lens.messianic_christological_trajectory: Matthew names Jesus Messiah and son of David and Abraham, develops Emmanuel, Son of God, Son of Man, teacher, healer, servant, king, crucified one, risen Lord, and abiding presence. Later Christology is genuine reception but must not be retrojected without argument.

hermeneutical_lens.historical_interpretation: Early reception strongly associated the Gospel with Matthew and made it central to teaching and liturgy. Patristic, medieval, Reformation, modern critical, Jewish-dialogical, liberationist, feminist, postcolonial, and other readers have emphasized different texts and exposed both generative and violent effects.
hermeneutical_lens.authorial_intent: The final narrator appears to present Jesus' identity, fulfillment, authoritative teaching and deeds, disputed reception, death, resurrection, and continuing commission. More specific biographical or communal intentions remain reconstructions.
typological_connections: Abraham, David, exile, and restored genealogy
Israel and son called from Egypt
Moses, wilderness, mountain, Torah, and covenant patterns
Davidic king, servant, Son of Man, temple, and shepherd imagery
Jonah, Solomon, Elijah, Jeremiah, Daniel, and prophetic trajectories
hermeneutical_lens.christological_significance: Christian theology receives Matthew as a major witness to incarnation, Messiah, divine sonship, teaching authority, atoning death, resurrection, universal authority, Father-Son-Spirit baptism, and abiding presence, while historical exegesis distinguishes text from later creedal development.
modern_application_principles: Interpret kingdom ethics with protection for victims and accountability for power.
Read Jewish conflict without antisemitism, supersessionism, or collective blame.
Practice mission without coercion, empire, cultural erasure, or forced baptism.
Treat bodies, disability, mental health, gender, sexuality, poverty, and family without stigma.
Reject date-setting, conspiracy theories, national prophecy maps, and partisan capture.
Let doubt, lament, trauma, women witnesses, children, outsiders, and economically vulnerable people remain visible.
common_misinterpretations: Matthew identifies its author or proves one exact date and city.
Fulfillment means Israel, Judaism, or Torah became obsolete.
Pharisee means hypocritical Jew and Matthew 27:25 curses all Jewish people.
Enemy love, forgiveness, divorce, family, or discipline require tolerating abuse.
Healing and exorcism equate disability or mental illness with sin or demons.
Peter, keys, binding, loosing, or discipline grant unaccountable clerical power.
Parables endorse slavery, exploitation, prosperity teaching, or blaming the poor.
Matthew 24 predicts a current headline or allows date-setting.
The Great Commission licenses colonialism, coercion, forced baptism, or religious violence.
Matthew 28:19 is either a complete Nicene doctrine or demonstrably a late Nicene manuscript insertion.
